primary.title: Trump Pardoned William E. Henry on January 19, 2021
primary.description_short: Trump pardoned William E. Henry on January 19, 2021, for a federal theft-of-government-property conviction.
primary.description_medium: The Justice Department lists William E. Henry under January 19, 2021 pardons, with the Middle District of Alabama, theft of government property, and a sentence of two years’ probation plus a $4,000 fine dated May 2, 2019. The listing does not state Trump’s reason for granting clemency.
primary.description_long: On January 19, 2021, Donald Trump granted a pardon to William E. Henry, whom the Department of Justice Office of the Pardon Attorney lists under that date. The official table names Henry, identifies the Middle District of Alabama, and lists theft of government property as the offense. It records two years’ probation and a $4,000 fine, with the sentence dated May 2, 2019. Those entries document the person, federal district, offense label, and sentence associated with the clemency grant. The table does not explain why Trump selected Henry, describe the conduct behind the conviction, or report an exchange or other private benefit. The fact of a pardon alone does not establish a corrupt motive. The supplied category “Corrupt Pardons” is not treated as evidence. Accordingly, this entry describes a documented presidential pardon while leaving motive and underlying case facts unknown. It makes no claim about financial loss, political favoritism, or public reaction.

frozen_original.synopsis: In a brazen display of corruption, Trump issued a wave of pardons in August 2025 targeting wealthy white-collar criminals and key political allies who had refused to cooperate with investigators. The pardons bypassed normal DOJ review processes and were heavily skewed toward individuals who had made substantial financial contributions to Trump's political committees.

primary.description_long: The supplied record alleges that Donald Trump issued a wave of pardons in August 2025 benefiting wealthy white-collar defendants and political allies, including people who had refused to cooperate with investigators. It further alleges that the grants bypassed normal Department of Justice review and favored people who had made substantial contributions to Trump’s political committees. These remain allegations supplied for drafting; this card does not present them as established events or findings. The prior research note states that it could not verify a discrete August 22 pardon wave matching the claim or evidence that the recipients were major Trump donors. No recipient names, pardon warrants, dated list of grants, donor matches, or review records are supplied here. A DOJ Office of the Pardon Attorney page listing clemency grants was located as a research reference, but the accessed search result did not establish the claimed August 22 group or the asserted financial relationships. Without records tying identified recipients to the same date and donor claim, the date, scale, motives, process, and beneficiary descriptions remain unresolved. Keep this draft unpublished until source material supports those specific allegations.

frozen_original.title: Hegseth Fires Top Military Officers Who Testified Against Trump in Impeachments
frozen_original.synopsis: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired multiple high-ranking military officers who had previously testified against Donald Trump during impeachment proceedings, purging the military of witnesses who went on record against the president. The firings targeted officers with distinguished careers who had testified truthfully before Congress, replacing institutional professionals with political loyalists. The purge represented a direct attack on military independence and the separation of civilian and military authority.

primary.title: Trump and Hegseth Remove Senior Military Leaders in February 2025
primary.description_short: Trump fired Joint Chiefs Chair C.Q. Brown; Hegseth also dismissed senior officers. The supplied impeachment-retaliation motive remains unsupported.
primary.description_medium: On February 21, 2025, President Donald Trump fired Joint Chiefs Chairman Air Force Gen. C.Q. Brown Jr. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth then fired Navy Adm. Lisa Franchetti and Air Force Gen. James Slife, according to AP reporting. Reuters described Brown and five other admirals and generals as pushed out in the leadership shake-up. The supplied impeachment-testimony motive is not established by these sources and is omitted from this corrected account.
primary.description_long: This corrected entry records a February 2025 change in senior U.S. military leadership. Reuters reported that President Donald Trump fired Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. C.Q. Brown on February 21 and described five other admirals and generals as pushed out in the same shake-up. The Associated Press reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth followed Brown’s dismissal by firing Navy Adm. Lisa Franchetti, then chief of naval operations, and Air Force Gen. James Slife, vice chief of the Air Force; AP also reported on changes to the services’ top military lawyers. The supplied record asserted that officers were removed because they testified against Trump in impeachment proceedings. The reporting reviewed for this corrected card documents who was dismissed, but does not establish that causal allegation or identify impeachment testimony as the reason. The account therefore names only the documented personnel actions and leaves motive unresolved. It does not characterize the changes as retaliation, a purge of witnesses, or proof of political loyalty. No conclusion about legality or resulting readiness effects is drawn. This correction preserves the dated leadership-change event while removing unsupported participants and motive.

frozen_original.title: Trump Calls Former AG Jeff Sessions 'Mentally Retarded' in Reported Comment
frozen_original.synopsis: In March 2020, The Atlantic reported that Trump had referred to his own former Attorney General Jeff Sessions using the term 'mentally retarded' in private conversations with advisers, a slur against people with intellectual disabilities that advocacy groups have long campaigned to eliminate from public usage. Trump had spent years publicly humiliating Sessions — calling him 'Mr. Magoo,' 'weak,' and 'pathetic' — for recusing himself from the Russia investigation. Trump's use of disability slurs fit a pattern that included mocking disabled reporter Serge Kovaleski, reportedly calling advisers 'retarded' in private, and attacking opponents' physical and cognitive characteristics. Disability rights groups condemned the reported language as demeaning to millions of Americans with intellectual disabilities.

primary.title: The Atlantic Reports a Woodward Book Allegation About Trump and Jeff Sessions
primary.description_short: A September 2018 report attributed a disability slur about then Attorney General Jeff Sessions to Bob Woodward’s forthcoming book about Trump.
primary.description_medium: On September 4, 2018, The Atlantic summarized excerpts from Bob Woodward’s forthcoming book Fear: Trump in the White House. It reported that the book quoted Trump using a disability slur about then Attorney General Jeff Sessions. This entry is dated to the sourced publication, not to the private remark; the sources do not establish when that conversation occurred or independently verify the quotation.
primary.description_long: An article The Atlantic published on September 4, 2018 summarized excerpts from Bob Woodward’s forthcoming book Fear: Trump in the White House. It described remarks in the book about several senior officials and said Trump referred to then Attorney General Jeff Sessions with a disability slur. CNN published a same-day report of the same book account, independently recording the allegation’s 2018 publication date and attribution. These sources establish that the allegation was reported and attributed to Woodward’s book; they do not establish the exact date of the private conversation or provide a recording or transcript. The frozen record assigns March 3, 2020 and attributes the claim to The Atlantic, but the specific Atlantic article located was published in 2018. The corrected date therefore identifies publication of the sourced report, not the date of an independently verified utterance. This copy keeps the statement attributed, does not present it as a judicial finding, and removes additional assertions about advocacy groups’ response, disability-rights impacts, or other alleged insults because no evidence for those claims was obtained in the supplied packet or sources accessed for this repair.
primary.date_basis: Publication date of the located Atlantic report; the source does not establish the exact date of the private conversation described in the book.
